# Oyakodon 🇯🇵

::: {.dish-meta}
**Region:** Japan  ·  **Family:** Simmer, served over rice
**Serves:** 2  ·  **Active time:** 20 minutes  ·  **Total:** 25 minutes
:::

The name *oyako* means "parent and child" — chicken and egg in the same bowl, a
gentle culinary pun that Japanese cooks have been making since the Meiji era.
It is the fastest dish in this book and, on a tired weeknight, maybe the most
comforting.

## The story

*Donburi* — a bowl of rice topped with something savory — is Japanese fast food
in the best sense. Oyakodon is said to have been born in the 1890s at Tamahide, a
Tokyo restaurant that specialized in chicken hot pot; the story goes that they
began serving the leftover chicken-and-egg simmer over rice for customers in a
hurry. Whatever the exact origin, it became a fixture of home kitchens and train
stations alike.

The whole thing hinges on one idea: the egg should be **just barely set**,
custardy and still trembling, folding the chicken and sweet-savory broth into the
hot rice beneath it.

## Ingredients

*Per serving — oyakodon is best cooked one portion at a time in a small pan.*

**The bowl**

- 1 boneless chicken thigh (~120 g), cut into bite-size pieces
- ¼ onion, thinly sliced
- 2 eggs, beaten *loosely* (streaks of white and yolk should remain)
- 1 scallion, sliced on the bias
- 1 generous bowl hot short-grain Japanese rice

**The simmering sauce (per serving)**

- 60 ml (¼ cup) dashi (use a **gluten-free** dashi — some instant granules contain wheat)
- 1 tbsp **gluten-free tamari** (in place of soy sauce)
- 1 tbsp mirin (choose a gluten-free brand)
- 1 tsp sugar
- 1 tsp sake (optional; naturally gluten-free)

**To finish:** shichimi togarashi, mitsuba or extra scallion

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Gluten-free · dairy-free:** naturally dairy-free. The gluten hides in the
seasonings — use gluten-free **tamari, mirin, and dashi**, and check that your
shichimi togarashi blend is gluten-free too.
:::

## Method

1. Whisk the dashi, soy, mirin, sugar, and sake in a small bowl.
2. Pour the sauce into a small (18–20 cm) non-stick or well-seasoned pan and bring
   to a simmer over medium heat.
3. Add the onion and simmer 2–3 minutes until softened and translucent.
4. Add the chicken in a single layer. Simmer 4–5 minutes, turning once, until
   just cooked through.
5. **Pour in about two-thirds of the beaten egg** in a swirl over the surface.
   Do not stir. Cover and cook 30–40 seconds until the edges begin to set.
6. Drizzle the remaining egg over the top, scatter the scallion, cover, and cook
   just 20–30 seconds more. **Kill the heat while the center is still glossy and
   loose** — carryover heat finishes it.
7. Slide the whole soft raft out of the pan onto a bowl of hot rice, letting the
   sauce soak in. Finish with shichimi and mitsuba.

## The one thing that matters

Restraint with the egg. Overcooked oyakodon — dry, rubbery, uniform yellow — is a
different and sadder dish. Beat the eggs loosely, add them in two stages, and pull
the pan while it still looks slightly underdone. It will be perfect by the time
it reaches the table.

## Make it yours

- **Katsudon** swaps the poached chicken for a crisp pork cutlet — same sauce,
  same egg technique.
- **Tanindon** ("stranger's bowl") uses beef instead of chicken, since beef and
  egg aren't "parent and child."
- No dashi on hand? Steep a small piece of kombu and a pinch of bonito in hot
  water for 10 minutes, or use a quality instant dashi granule.

::: {.callout-note}
## On dashi
Dashi — the kombu-and-bonito stock that underpins Japanese cooking — is worth
making well. It's a 15-minute infusion, not a long simmer, and it gives the dish
its clean, savory backbone.
:::
